newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T shares down after U.S. tobacco deal.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T shares down after U.S. tobacco deal.

text.p: Shares in B.A.T Industries Plc opened lower on Monday after the company said it expected its Brown & Williamson unit to make an initial payment of around $1.7 billion under a landmark U.S. tobacco settlement.
The shares fell 17p to 572p by 0748 GMT.

Under the agreement between U.S. states and the industry announced on Friday, tobacco companies will pay $368.5 billion over 25 years in compensation for the cost of treating smoking-related illnesses in return for immunity from further litigation.
Analysts said tobbaco shares, which have been dogged by the threat of escalating legal claims, will eventually show relief.
But recent speculation that an industry-wide deal was imminent had already brought BAT shares up from their lows.

"Sometimes its just better to travel than to arrive," said Simon Willis, industry analyst at Charterhouse Tilney, referring to today's bout of profit-taking on the settlement news after recent speculative buying.

"Tobacco shares have been quite buoyant over the last few weeks and we have to bear in mind that this proposed deal still has to go through Congress," Willis said. "The companies have got the best deal they can get and if the deal is altered at all in this process, it can only get worse."
Willis still expects the share price to climb through the six pounds level.
"We could see the shares trade up to 630p on a successful deal and the prospect of a demerger is the icing on the cake."
Analysts expect B.A.T to turn its attention now to a demerger of its tobacco and insurance businesses in an effort to boost shareholder value.
"But I think a demerger was much more likely when the share price was nearer five pounds than six," Willis said.

B.A.T's Brown & Williamson is the third largest cigarette-maker in the U.S., with brands such as Kent and Lucky Strike. But shares in Imperial Tobacco and Gallaher Group, which do not have the same exposure to U.S. litigation, were also sharply lower on Monday.

Imperial fell 10p to 395p and shares in Gallaher, Britain's largest cigarette maker were 6-1/2p lower at 293p. "The shares have fallen on the prospect that the class action in the UK could gain momentum on the back of this deal," Willis said.
"There is also the prospect that the UK will try and recover its healthcare costs and the likelihood of strong tax rises in the Budget (on July 2)," Willis added.
Gallaher, which was floated on the London stock market last month, manufactures Benson and Hedges and Silk Cut brands of cigarettes. Imperial's brands include Lambert & Butler and Embassy.
